title: The more laws
hook: the more prohibitions, the poorer the people; I do nothing and they change themselves (Tao Te Ching 57)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was who knows doesn't speak: the knower closes the mouth and softens the glare. Your line was who knows is quiet.

Taped to the fridge in a shared apartment: label your food. Below it, in different handwriting: and wash your dishes the same day. Below that: no dishes in the sink overnight, this means you. Then: who used my oat milk. By the end of the semester the fridge door is a wall of notes, the sink is full, and nobody speaks to anybody in the kitchen. More rules went up, and the place got worse. Chapter fifty-seven of the Tao Te Ching saw this pattern long before refrigerators, and wrote it at the size of a whole kingdom.
screen: `A FRIDGE DOOR OF RULES.` → `MORE NOTES, WORSE KITCHEN.` → `THE SAME PATTERN, KINGDOM SIZE.`

segments.voice: First, three ways to hold power. A state is governed by what's correct, the chapter says, and a war is fought with surprise. But the world itself is won by not meddling. Second, the list. The more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people become. The more sharp tools people have, the more disorder in the land. The more cleverness, the more strange contraptions. The more laws are put on display, the more thieves and robbers appear. It's a run of mores, and each one backfires. Third, the sage's answer. In James Legge's translation, a sage has said: "I will do nothing (of purpose), and the people will be transformed of themselves." The chapter goes on in the same rhythm: the sage loves stillness, and the people settle themselves. The sage doesn't meddle, and they prosper. The sage wants nothing, and they return to simplicity. Readers take this more than one way. Some read it as political advice: govern lightly. Others read it closer to home, about anyone with a little authority over anyone else. Fourth, smaller kingdoms. A parent with a rule for everything. A manager who answers every mistake with a new policy. A partner keeping a quiet rulebook the other person never saw. The chapter isn't saying no one should ever set a limit. Read this way, it raises a sharper question: does this rule make things better, or does it just make you feel in control?
screen: `THE WORLD IS WON BY NOT MEDDLING.` · `THE MORE PROHIBITIONS, THE POORER.` · `THE SAGE DOES NOTHING; THEY CHANGE.` · `CARE, OR CONTROL?` · then, large: `TRANSFORMED OF THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you have some say over, at home, at work, on a team, and quietly list a few of the rules you keep for them, spoken or unspoken: how the towels get folded, when someone should text back. Find one rule that's more about your comfort than their good, and picture a day without it. Notice what tightens, and what eases.
The more laws. Chapter fifty-seven: the more prohibitions, the poorer the people, and the more laws on display, the more thieves. The sage meddles less, and people change of themselves. Today's word.
Your line: fewer rules. A fridge with one note may be the calmer kitchen. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter fifty-seven both as advice to rulers to govern lightly and as a personal teaching for anyone with authority: meddle less, and let people settle themselves.

fork.setup: you govern a restless land. thefts are up and people are poor. what does chapter fifty-seven's sage do?
options: do less, keep still, and let people settle.
fork.reveal: the sage does nothing of purpose and loves stillness, and the people are transformed of themselves and grow settled and prosperous.

chat.says: Is the chapter saying nobody should ever set any rules?
options: No; it questions piling them on: the more laws on display, the more thieves appear.
Yes; it says every rule is wrong and people should live with none at all.
No; it says a wise ruler adds a new rule for every new problem that comes.

Paraphrases of chapter 57: the opening triad (state by correctness, war by surprise, world by non-meddling) and the list of 'mores' follow the received Chinese text; Legge's wording differs (e.g. 'freedom from action and purpose'). Confirm the paraphrase is fair.
'Sharp tools' renders 利器; readers translate it as weapons or profitable implements. Confirm.
